beats.headline: Why does Java reject List<Integer> as a List<Number>?
beats.subline: It isn't a bug—it's a critical safety feature to prevent heap pollution.
beats.narration: If Java allowed you to treat a List of Integers as a List of Numbers, you could silently insert a Double into that list. Generics are invariant to stop this at compile time.

beats.title: Arrays vs. Generics

top.label: Arrays (Covariant)

bottom.label: Generics (Invariant)

beats.narration: Arrays are covariant and reified, meaning they know their type at runtime, which leads to crashes. Generics are invariant and erased, stopping the error before you even run the code.

beats.title: The Erasure Pipeline
beats.subtitle: How javac strips type safety
beats.narration: During compilation, javac enforces your types, then erases them. It replaces T with its bound, like Object, and inserts checkcast instructions to keep your runtime safe.

beats.title: Synthetic Bridge Methods

steps.explanation: Extending a generic class requires bridge methods.
javac adds this to keep virtual dispatch working.

beats.narration: Because of erasure, the parent expects Object, but the child expects String. javac silently injects a bridge method to bridge the gap and maintain polymorphism.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Generics are invariant to ensure safety
Type erasure removes T at runtime
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Mastering PECS and Wildcards →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we decode the PECS mnemonic to stop fighting the compiler when using wildcards.

beats.headline: Why does List<? extends Number> forbid adding numbers?
beats.subline: It’s not a compiler bug—it’s a guarantee against heap corruption.
beats.narration: You can read from a List of extends Number, but you can't add to it. Why? Because the compiler can't guarantee the list isn't actually a List of Doubles.

beats.title: PECS Mnemonic
beats.subtitle: The golden rule for variance
beats.narration: Remember PECS. If your method produces values, use extends. If it consumes values, use super. If it does both, stick to an exact type.

beats.title: Applying PECS

steps.explanation: Dest receives data, so we use super.
Src provides data, so we use extends.

beats.narration: The Collections copy method is the perfect example. It copies from a producer source to a consumer destination, using both wildcards to maximize flexibility.

beats.title: The Write-Only Trap
beats.caption: Why List<? extends Number> is read-only

lines.text: List<? extends Number> list = new ArrayList<Double>();
# Compiler blocks this to prevent adding

beats.narration: The compiler blocks writes here because it doesn't know the specific subtype. If it allowed an Integer add, you'd crash the JVM with a ClassCastException later.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Bounded Types & Recursive Bounds →
beats.narration: PECS is your best friend. In Part 3, we look at bounded type parameters and how to handle recursive bounds like Comparable.

beats.headline: Why is <T extends Comparable<? super T>> so common?
beats.subline: It's the secret to making your generic collections truly flexible.
beats.narration: Ever wonder why the max method in collections is so complex? It’s because simple bounds fail when you use inheritance. Let's break down recursive bounds.

beats.title: Multiple Bounds
beats.code:
<T extends Number & Comparable<T> & Serializable>
T clamp(T value) { ... }

steps.explanation: The class must always come before interfaces.

beats.narration: You can enforce multiple bounds with the ampersand. Just remember: the class must be listed first, or the compiler will reject your code.

beats.title: Recursive Bound Flexibility
beats.narration: The flexible bound allows a class to compare itself against a supertype. This is why it's the standard for library APIs—it just works with inheritance.

beats.title: Erasure with Bounds
beats.subtitle: What happens to T?
beats.narration: When you bound a type, erasure doesn't go to Object. It goes to your leftmost bound. The compiler inserts casts to ensure you can safely call methods on that type.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Class must be the first bound
Comparable super T is the standard
beats.narration: Bounds keep your generics predictable. In Part 4, we tackle heap pollution and the dangerous world of varargs.

beats.headline: Can a List<String> contain an Integer?
beats.subline: Yes, through heap pollution. And it will crash your app at runtime.
beats.narration: Heap pollution is the silent killer of type safety. By mixing raw types and generics, you can bypass the compiler and store the wrong type in a list.

beats.title: The Pollution Path
beats.code:
List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List raw = strings; // Raw type bypass
raw.add(42);        // Heap is now polluted
String s = strings.get(0); // ClassCastException!

steps.explanation: The cast happens here, not at the add.

beats.narration: Using raw types is the primary way to pollute the heap. The compiler can't stop you, but the JVM will throw a ClassCastException when you try to read the data.

beats.title: Why @SafeVarargs?

steps.explanation: Promises the method won't corrupt the array.
Varargs are just arrays under the hood.

beats.narration: Varargs are just arrays. Since arrays are covariant, they can be unsafe. Use @SafeVarargs only if you promise not to write to or leak that array.

beats.title: Varargs Safety

top.label: Unsafe Varargs

bottom.label: Safe Varargs

beats.narration: If you leak the array or write to it, you're creating a trap. Only mark methods as SafeVarargs if they strictly read the input.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
beats.narration: Safety first. In Part 5, we see how libraries like Jackson recover generic types at runtime using Super Type Tokens.

beats.headline: How does Jackson know you want a List<User>?
beats.subline: Generics are erased, but the metadata is still hiding in the class file.
beats.narration: If generics are erased at runtime, how do JSON libraries deserialize into specific types? It’s a clever trick called Super Type Tokens.

beats.title: The Magic Trick

steps.explanation: The {} creates a subclass with metadata.
The generic type is stored in the class signature.

beats.narration: By using an anonymous subclass, the generic type information is baked into the class signature, which reflection can read at runtime.

beats.title: Recovering Types
beats.subtitle: How reflection reads the signature
beats.narration: Reflection reads the superclass signature from the bytecode. It finds the ParameterizedType, allowing it to extract the exact generic arguments you provided.

beats.title: When It Fails
beats.caption: The limitation of tokens

lines.text: # T is a variable, not a concrete type.
# Reflection only sees the variable T.

beats.narration: This only works if the type is concrete. If you try it with a generic type variable, you'll just get the variable back, not the actual runtime class.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Super Type Tokens store types in signatures
